title: Data Carving: Concepts & Methods
description: Carve files from unallocated space using headers, footers, and smart carving algorithms.

slides.title: When Metadata Fails 🚫
slides.content:
# Enter the Carver

Data carving is the process of extracting files from a raw data stream (unallocated space, memory dumps) without the help of file system metadata. It relies on:

- **Header/Footer signatures**: Most file types start with a specific byte sequence (magic bytes) and some end with a footer.
- **File structure**: Carvers can validate the internal structure to reduce false positives.

Carving is your last resort – but often finds the most hidden evidence.

quizData.question: Data carving is most useful when:

options.text: The file system is fully intact
File system metadata has been destroyed or is unavailable
You need a quick listing of active files
You are working on a write‑blocked original

quizData.explanation: Carving bypasses the file system entirely, making it essential when directory entries or MFT records are missing.

slides.title: Header/Footer Carving 🪓
slides.content:
## Simple but Effective

Search for a known header (e.g., `FF D8 FF` for JPEG). Then extract data until a known footer (`FF D9` for JPEG) or until a maximum size is reached.

| File Type | Header | Footer |
|-----------|--------|--------|
| JPEG | FF D8 FF | FF D9 |
| PNG | 89 50 4E 47 | 49 45 4E 44 AE 42 60 82 |
| PDF | 25 50 44 46 | 25 25 45 4F 46 |
| ZIP | 50 4B 03 04 | (none, end of central directory) |

Some formats lack footers; carvers rely on a new header or max size to stop.

slides.title: Carve JPEGs with Foremost
slides.content: Foremost reads raw data and outputs files sorted by type.
slides.codeSnippet:
foremost -t jpeg -i unallocated.bin -o /recovered/
# -t : file type (jpeg, pdf, etc.)
# -i : input
# -o : output folder

quizData.question: The hexadecimal footer for a JPEG file is ___.
quizData.explanation: JPEG files end with the marker FF D9 (End of Image).

slides.title: Fragmented Files & Smart Carving 🧩
slides.content:
## The Fragmentation Problem

Files on disk are not always stored contiguously. If a JPEG is split across non‑adjacent clusters, simple header‑footer carving fails.

**Smart carving** uses validation techniques:
- Check internal structures (e.g., JPEG restart markers).
- Use a block‑by‑block validation (what if this cluster is part of the previous file?).
- Graph‑based carving (assign probabilities of cluster belonging to a file).

Tools like **PhotoRec** perform some validation but may still struggle with heavy fragmentation. Manual reassembly is sometimes necessary.

quizData.question: A simple header‑footer carver can perfectly recover fragmented files.
quizData.explanation: If a file is fragmented, pieces may be separated by other data; a simple carver will miss or truncate it.

slides.title: PhotoRec – A Powerful Carver 🖼️
slides.content:
PhotoRec (part of TestDisk) can carve over 480 file types. It scans sectors for signatures, and if a footer exists, tries to extract the full file. For file types without footers, it stops after a threshold.

Usage: `photorec /image.dd` then select partition and output folder.

It's fast, reliable, and often recovers files even after formatting.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Combine Carving with String Search

Before carving, run `strings` or a keyword search on unallocated space to identify interesting content. Then target specific file types for carving.
